h1: Milvus vs pgvector: a vector database comparison for growing data
intro: pgvector adds vector search to Postgres, keeping relational data, transactions and joins together. It scales through larger instances, read replicas or additional sharding systems. Milvus is a dedicated vector database with object storage and separately scalable ingest, indexing and query resources. Choose by relational requirements and measured filtering, throughput, latency and operating needs.

sections.h2: Milvus vs pgvector scalability: what happens when the table outgrows one Postgres box?
paragraphs: Milvus is built on storage-compute separation. Segments and the write-ahead log live in object storage, so a new query node loads its assigned segments instead of copying another node's disk, and ingestion, search and indexing each scale on separate node types. Tiered storage lets a node serve more data than fits in its memory and disk.

pgvector scalability is Postgres scalability. Its README says to scale vertically by adding memory, CPU and storage to one instance, and horizontally with replicas or a sharding layer such as Citus or PgDog. Postgres replicas are read-only, so every write and every HNSW build runs on the primary, and HNSW builds slow down once the graph no longer fits in maintenance_work_mem.

sections.h2: pgvector vs Milvus features: index types, filtering and hybrid search
paragraphs: pgvector gives Postgres two ANN index types and the full SQL toolbox around them. Milvus is a purpose-built vector database: more index families, scalar indexes that filter before the vector search, and a server-side BM25 function with built-in rankers for hybrid search. The table is the quickest vector database comparison for the decision.

sections.h2: Is Milvus harder to set up than pgvector?
paragraphs: Milvus Lite starts in-process from pip; CPU is the default and GPU indexes are optional. Existing Postgres teams can start with pgvector and later reuse embeddings when model and dimensions match, but migration still requires schema mapping, index creation and query changes. Size both systems for index memory, storage, traffic and availability.

sections.h2: When is pgvector the better choice?
paragraphs: pgvector reuses the transactions, joins and operating model of an existing Postgres deployment. Decide whether to migrate from measured index, filtering and scaling needs; its scaling options also include read replicas and sharding systems such as Citus or PgDog.
bullets: Your data already lives in Postgres and the vector table is small enough for one primary.
You need ACID transactions or JOINs between embeddings and relational rows.
Agent memory or checkpoints with transactional updates; pair it with Milvus for the large retrieval corpus.
You run a managed Postgres (RDS, Supabase, Neon) and want no new service to operate.
Your team works in SQL and prefers one connection string over a new client library.

The README sets no row limit; capacity is the primary's. HNSW builds fast only while the graph fits maintenance_work_mem, every replica is a full copy, and growth past one box means Citus or PgDog sharding. Milvus Standalone is documented to about 100 million vectors and Distributed to tens of billions.

Yes, by combining a vector query with Postgres full-text search (tsvector) and fusing the two result sets with Reciprocal Rank Fusion in SQL or application code. Milvus runs the BM25 function server-side and fuses dense and sparse results in one hybrid_search call with RRF or weighted rankers.
When should I use pgvector instead of Milvus?

Milvus or pgvector depends on where the data lives and how fast it grows. Pick pgvector when the vectors sit next to relational rows you join and update transactionally, and the table fits one Postgres instance. Pick Milvus when scale, filtering throughput or tenant count is the constraint.
Is pgvector good enough for production RAG?

For a single-tenant corpus on an existing Postgres, yes: HNSW with iterative index scans handles filtered retrieval. pgvector limitations show up as the corpus grows: HNSW on vector is capped at 2,000 dimensions, index builds need maintenance_work_mem, and reads only scale through full replicas.
How hard is migrating from pgvector to Milvus later?

It is a copy. VTS lists Postgres Vector as a source (pg_to_milvus), so embeddings and columns move without re-embedding. Map columns to scalar or JSON fields, build indexes in Milvus, dual-write from the same source, and keep relational tables in Postgres joined by primary key.
